c.tagline: Romania's ancient Black Sea port, from Roman Tomis to the Mamaia beach strip.

taxi.fareNote: Licensed taxis are metered with the rate posted on the door; app-hailing via Bolt or Uber is common and avoids fare disputes.

emergency.note: 112 is the single EU-wide emergency number connecting to police, ambulance and fire.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Watch belongings on crowded Mamaia beaches and in summer nightlife clubs, where petty theft and inflated taxi fares are the main risks.

hood_desc: The historic peninsula around Ovid Square, home to the Roman mosaic edifice, the landmark (long-derelict, now restored) seafront Casino, the Grand Mosque and the ancient roots of Tomis; atmospheric, walkable and packed with Constanța's headline sights.

The lively downtown spine along Bulevardul Tomis and Ștefan cel Mare, with shopping, the City Park Mall, cafes, restaurants and the National History and Archaeology Museum nearby; a central, convenient base year-round.

The long sandy resort strip on a spit between the sea and Lake Siutghiol just north of the city, wall-to-wall with hotels, beach clubs, the Aqua Magic water park and Romania's busiest summer nightlife.
The northern clifftop seafront (faleza) of newer residential blocks and hotels overlooking the Black Sea; calmer than Mamaia but still an easy tram or bus ride to the beaches and center.
A large, mostly residential district north of the center with everyday shops, parks and local restaurants; quiet and good value, popular with those wanting a non-touristy base.

water.note: Tap water is safe, though many locals prefer bottled for taste.

transit.hours: City buses run roughly 5:00 AM to 11:00 PM, with extra summer services and a seasonal tourist line along Mamaia; taxis and Bolt/Uber cover the late hours.
transit.note: Constanța has no metro or tram-rail; the CT Bus network is the backbone, including frequent routes out to Mamaia. In summer a beach-front tourist bus and the Mamaia cable car (telegondola) add scenic options.
transit.pay: Buses take contactless bank cards tapped on board, or the rechargeable CT Bus card and single tickets bought from machines and kiosks; validate on boarding.

bus: Autogări with intercity & FlixBus coaches to Bucharest and the coast
train: CFR Călători trains (Constanța Gara) to Bucharest, Mangalia and Mamaia

transit.m: Bus 540 to the city center (~40-50 min)
Taxi or ride-hail to the center (25-35 min)

tip.r: Around 10% at restaurants for good service; rounding up taxi fares is appreciated.

landmarks: Constanța Casino
An extravagant Art Nouveau casino of 1910 poised on the Black Sea promenade, this recently restored seashell-windowed icon is Romania's most romantic seaside landmark.
Roman Edifice with Mosaic
A vast 4th-century Roman commercial complex preserves over 800 square meters of polychrome mosaic floor, terraced dramatically above the ancient port of Tomis.
National History and Archaeology Museum and Ovid Square
Fronted by the brooding statue of exiled poet Ovid, the museum treasures the enigmatic Glykon serpent statue and Tomis's ancient sculptures.
Great Mahmudiye Mosque (Carol I Mosque)
Built in 1913 for the sultan's former subjects, its 47-meter minaret rewards climbers with the definitive panorama over the peninsula and harbor.
Genoese Lighthouse
An 1860 stone lighthouse honoring the Genoese merchants who navigated these waters in the Middle Ages, standing photogenically at the tip of the old town promenade.
Saints Peter and Paul Orthodox Cathedral
Constanța's 1885 brick cathedral rises near the seafront, its Byzantine-Romanian interior rebuilt after wartime bombing and rich with neo-Byzantine murals.
Old Town peninsula and seafront promenade
Faded Ottoman, Greek, and Art Nouveau facades line the Tomis peninsula's lanes, ending in a breezy esplanade above the sparkling Black Sea.
Mamaia
Romania's flagship beach resort stretches along a sandbar just north of the city, eight kilometers of fine sand, beach clubs, and a panoramic gondola lift.
Constanța Aquarium
Facing the Casino on the seafront, Romania's oldest public aquarium showcases Black Sea species, sturgeons, and exotic fish in a compact historic setting.
Constanța Dolphinarium
A seaside marine park on Bulevardul Mamaia with a covered amphitheatre where bottlenose dolphins, sea lions and penguins perform for daily shows.

train.note: CFR Călători InterCity and regional trains link Constanța Gara with Bucharest in about 2-2.5 hours; summer services run down the coast to Mangalia and shuttle to Mamaia.

bus.note: Intercity coaches and FlixBus depart from Constanța's autogări for Bucharest, Tulcea and the southern Black Sea resorts.

ferry.note: Constanța is primarily a major commercial cargo port; there are no scheduled international passenger ferries, but Tomis Marina runs summer pleasure and excursion boats along the coast.

full.blurb: Europe's largest surviving wetland and a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, reached via Tulcea (~2 hr) for boat trips through channels teeming with birdlife.
full.name: Danube Delta (via Tulcea)

full.blurb: A monumental Roman victory memorial and ruined city about 60 km southwest commemorating Trajan's Dacian campaigns, with an adjacent museum.
full.name: Adamclisi (Tropaeum Traiani)

half.blurb: The ruins of the oldest Greek colony on Romanian soil, founded around 657 BC, spread beside a lagoon about 60 km north with a small on-site museum.
half.name: Histria (Cetatea Histria)

half.blurb: A saltwater lake about 18 km south famed for its therapeutic black sapropel mud, with lakeside spa resorts and the town of Eforie nearby.
half.name: Techirghiol Lake & Mud Baths

half.blurb: A classic Black Sea beach town just south of the city with wide sands, a promenade and easy train/bus access — an easy swim-and-relax outing.
half.name: Eforie Nord
